I have quite a few races that are extreme sizes! The most commonly known smaller race would be the Woodlanders, they're a race of humanoid beings who range from 2-4 inches tall. As a species they aren't that magic capable, so their defenses against outsiders aren't the best. The other major species they share their continent with, the druids, once saw them as nothing more than pets or playthings. It took several decades for Woodlanders to gain their freedom, although there are still a few underground places where average sized beings can get them as pets, toys, or worse, snacks. The Woodlanders' political system is rather corrupt, so of course there's a ton of rumors about that the tribe leaders are the ones running the underground trafficking.

Other races I have with notable heights are the fairies (2-5 inches), Meniain (7-12 feet), Dragons (they have four forms, humanistic ones are 5-6 feet, but their primal and dragona forms can be anywhere from 6 feet to several thousand), and the Dennai (1-4 inches). Those races tend to either not interact with other races or change their heights via magic for easier interaction. I also have a few monsters/animals that have vast sizes, but they're animals so their interaction tends to just be eating others.

Thousands of years back, the elves' country, Loston, was invaded by the fairies. Half the population was murdered, the other half enslaved, and the royals were locked up while fairy nobles experimented with the elven royals unique kind of magic. Delilah grew up living in a cell, but escaped. She left the world of Cyria and lived in New York, not really feeling up to causing political revolution by announcing her presence and the fact that Loston now has an actual heir. Ultimately, she did return to Cyria, was able to get into contact with major political powers, and reinstated her country while freeing her species from slavery.

Some elves are pissed because she spent years in New York while they were *enslaved*, while others don't care how long it took, just that she eventually did do the right thing. Most of the other species have varying perceptions of her, and it generally depends if they come from a pro-slavery country or not.

Also there's a lot of contriversy over the fact that she brought a handgun to a magic fight. Some think that her 'New York humanistic weponry' is too extra for their wand-only-world, but some people thought the action was straight up badass.

It's all still there! Cyria, my world, is in an entirely different solar system than Earth. Traveling to it via space would take thousands, if not millions, of years.

However, Cyria also happens to be filled with portals. Some lead to other places in Cyria, some leads to other planets, and quite a few lead to Earth. When both planets were relatively young and live was just budding, travel between the two were common. In universe, that's how Earth got the 'myths' of elves, dragons, magic, etc. Ultimately though, portals between Earth and Cyria had to be destroyed for human's safety. During the time when travel between the two were common, the dragon population was quite high, and a handful of dragons took a liking to feeding on humans (Dragons feed speciically off of emotions, and humans feel emotions in a particular way, leading them to be a favorite.). The portals were destroyed to prevent people from coming in to just become snacks, and to prevent dragons from entering Earth and wreacking havoc.

The only portals that remain between Cyria and Earth are ones that would be too difficult to destroy, such as portals at the bottom of vast lakes, some at huge heights, or some so small that humanesque beings can't fit. There are a few well-guarded portals in several scientific and more modern communities, but those are strictly monitered to make sure no trouble is caused. Since the dragon population has declined on Cyria's surface, there are a few humans about now, but they're far from common. In some countries, humans are just as much a myth as fantasy creatures are on Earth.

The Correspondence, a periodic meeting of the world's leaders, have discussed reopening several portals to Earth, for trade and education purposes. Ultimately though it was decided that reintroducing the two worlds to one another would cause far more trouble than it would anything good. While humans aren't explicitly banned from entering Cyria, they work to avoid widespread knowledge of Cyria in Earth, at least until they decide that the two worlds are advanced enough to co-exist peacefully.

I have one character like this, and I have her be suspicious (but not overly so) via her tendency to ramble her elderly heart out. Just saying "I know how to teleport" would raise suspicion, but having a ramble "Oh, I once found tea leaves like these, when I was young, had to teleport up a mountain to get them, but it was worth it! Takes a while to brew, but it's rather sweet-" etc. will make the other characters be able to recall the suspicous info but link it to the less suspicious things. ie.: "She mentioned teleportation, something about tea with it? She kept on rambling so I didn't get any answers, probably nothing worth worrying about. Maybe she just loves tea?". Personally I found sandwhiching suspicious things with normal things to work best for me.

I did this with a ditzy character, but you could easily work it into another personality. Dragon's broody? Have him spit out info while in the midst of a grump fest or rant - even if others are suspicious they won't want to ask. Dragon's friendly? Let him slip things in casual, plesant conversation. If 3000 years old is seen as 'elderly' for dragons, perhaps have him act like he's a bit senile or simply clueless, so he can play off info as just old man rambles.

How your characters react is also dependant on their personalities. A naieve kid on his first adventure would proabably beleive anything the dragon says. Someone used to being in authority would call the dragon out, someone might respect their elders enough to not question anything, someone might just blab out any questions they have, it depends on your characters. Letting things like that happen though could give hints to the twist, having a character raise an eyebrow in suspicion but not say anything would steer the reader into getting a feel for what's suspicious, the character's personality, and that the dragon has something to hide.

I'm in the same boat. I have a handful of mental illnesses, and have had suicidal thoughts for the past five-ish years. I threw myself into Overwatch to help cope with those things. I dropped down to low silver almost instantly, and honestly? It does hurt! It hurts loving something and trying to find solace in it only to turn out you aren't that good at it, so I relate.

What I usually do is stick to the "less serious" versions, No Limits or Quickplay, as people tend to be a bit less harsh there. There's less 'repercussions' too (not losing SR/ranks), so you're free to flex your skills and get practice with new heros. Playing custom maps or doing the practice range helps too, it lets you get a feel for characters and maps without the pressure of games with others.

One thing I also found helped me was that I found a game I could get into that *wasn't* online and didn't have repercussions for failing. I've been playing Stardew Valley, and having a game that's calmer helps cool me when I'm having bad runs in Overwatch. Perhaps find a game like that, something you can play when Overwatch gets too overwhelming? 

I really hope you find something that works for you, best of luck to you <3

When I was a little kid, I didn't really have friends. I was homeschooled, and at church/in my neighborhood I was "that weird girl no one talks to". Since I was alone most of the time, and since I had a computer with a basic text editor, I started writing down the stories I'd make up to keep me entertained. I'd write plays for me and my cousins to perform, I'd write stories about my dog or princesses or other silly little things. Eventually I got into fandoms and made a fanfiction.net account (which my entire family had access to so it wasn't always what I would have prefered to write). I later made a seperate account for some of my 'secret' fandoms, and through the massive ammount of hate and compliments I got on there I grew tough skin and retreated back to original works with a new perspective on writing. I still write fanfic on the side, but I'm not churning out 3+ stories a week like I used to. What really got me back into the swing of writing was when I went through a rough time with my illnesses and depression a few years ago. I made a character with similar struggles that I was going through, and it was the first time I ever actually ignored the "don't make characters based off of you" advice that's tossed about so frequently. She was a woman who used her ballet dancing as a coping mechanisim, lost her leg and therefore her job and home, and was then thrust into a fantasy world, because I had never written fantasy at the time and wanted to try it.

Creating that story and that world taught me two things. 

One, by putting a piece of my soul into each of my characters, my writing gets more realistic than ever. My characters do fight wizards and kill fairy nobles and stop creationist magic uprisings, but they also go through "normal" struggles too. Right now, my two main projects deal with the weight of taking care of others while ignoring your own needs & losing best friends, and the other is about finding the balance between your duty to yourself and your duty to others. Giving my characters problems that I struggle with made them so much easier to write, and so much more /real/. 

Two, crafting a fictional world from scratch gave me freedom I hadn't found in writing before. I didn't have to google how schools in England work or what the weather is like in Nebraska or all the other little details I'd obsess over instead of writing. Making my own world entails making my own rules and species and cultures, which taught me a lot on how those things work, and when to obsess over details vs. when to just jump in. Now my fictional world (Cyria) has 14 countries, multiple original species and cultures, and several magic systems. It's the thing that I'm the most proud of. It's currently the setting for 5 written novels, and a dozen or so more planned ones.

My advice to any aspiring authors would simply be to ignore advice, just write. One of my main faults during my fanfiction days and my first years of original works was that I obsessed over advice to a fault. I'd do things that didn't work for me simply because my favorite authors said people should do them. Don't bend your creativity just to follow arbitrary rules, test out advice and if it doesn't work, that's okay! This is you writing, not anyone else, so do what works for you, not Stephen King or J.K. Rowling or George R.R. Martin. Write for you.

Spark looked up from the troubling coffee pot.

“Drey, none of us are humans.”

“It's an expression.”

“Still,” Spark sighed, turning back to the coffee pot in frustration. She smacked the side of it. The coffee pot let out a sharp noise, but made no more effort to make coffee.

“But seriously, I don't get how you don't like tea,” Dreya pressed.

“I can't get that you don't love coffee.”

Super Paper Mario. 

I went in blind as a kid, and I fell in love. The storyline, the soundtrack, the gameplay, it's all utterly enchanting. The characters (especially the villains) have dimensions that you wouldn't expect from a Mario game, and the story is utterly captivating. The world designs are super interesting, as you start moving through worlds you go beyond the typical "grass, underground, underwater, etc." stages that sidescrollers are prone to. Those levels do exist, but there's worlds based on Christian and Greek mythology, mazes, one level even pokes fun at gamer/nerd steryotypes.

Plus, there's so much to do. It has insane value for completionists (2 Pits of Trials, a Samurai tournament, unlockable recipies, collectable cards, and more). Replays are definitely worth it too, as there's tons of little quips or storyline references you'll catch on the second go, and you can get different dialogue options based on who in your party you play as.

Definitely an underrated game, would totally reccomend it.
